blocks.p: Moreover, I saw in my dream that as they went on, Faithful happened to glance to one side and saw a man named Talkative walking along at a distance beside them, for in this place there was room enough for all of them to walk. He was a tall man, and somewhat better looking from far away than up close. Faithful spoke to him.
“Friend, where are you headed? Are you going to the heavenly country?”
“I’m going to the same place,” said Talkative.
“Good. Then I hope we may have your company.”
“With all my heart, I’ll be your companion.”
“Come on, then,” said Faithful, “let’s go together, and spend our time talking about things that are worthwhile.”

“To talk about good things is very welcome to me,” said Talkative, “with you or with anyone else, and I’m glad to have met people who are inclined to such good work. To tell the truth, there are few who care to spend their time this way as they travel. Most would much rather talk about things of no use at all, and that has been a trouble to me.”
“That is indeed something to regret,” said Faithful. “For what is more worthy of a man’s tongue and mouth here on earth than the things of the God of heaven?”

“I like you enormously, for what you say is full of conviction. And I’ll add: what is so pleasant, and so profitable, as to talk about the things of God? What is so delightful, that is, if a man has any taste for the wonderful? If a man loves to talk of history, or of the mystery of things, or of miracles, wonders, and signs, where will he find them recorded so delightfully, and so beautifully written, as in the Holy Scriptures?”
“That’s true,” said Faithful. “But to be helped by such things in our talk should be what we aim for.”

“That’s just what I said. To talk of such things is most profitable, because by doing so a man may gain knowledge of many things: in general, of the emptiness of earthly things and the benefit of things above; and in particular, of the necessity of the new birth, the insufficiency of our own works, the need of Christ’s righteousness, and so on. By talk, a man may also learn what it is to repent, to believe, to pray, to suffer, and the like. He may learn the great promises and comforts of the gospel, to his own encouragement. And further, he may learn to refute false opinions, to defend the truth, and to instruct the ignorant.”
“All this is true, and I’m glad to hear it from you.”

“Alas, it’s the lack of this that explains why so few understand the need for faith, and the necessity of a work of grace in their souls if they are to have eternal life. Instead, they live in ignorance, trying to earn heaven by keeping the law, which no one can ever do.”
“But if you’ll allow me,” said Faithful, “heavenly knowledge of these things is the gift of God. No one gets it by human effort, or merely by talking about it.”
“I know all that very well. A man can receive nothing unless it is given him from heaven; it’s all of grace, not of works. I could give you a hundred scriptures to prove it.”
“Well, then,” said Faithful, “what is the one thing we should build our conversation on right now?”

“Whatever you like. I’ll talk of things heavenly or things earthly; things moral or things evangelical; things sacred or things profane; things past or things to come; things foreign or things at home; things essential or things incidental; so long as it’s all to our profit.”

Now Faithful began to marvel. He stepped over to Christian, who had been walking by himself all this while, and said to him quietly, “What a fine companion we’ve found! This man will surely make an excellent pilgrim.”
At this Christian smiled a little and said, “This man you’re so taken with will deceive, with that tongue of his, twenty people who don’t know him.”
“Do you know him, then?”
“Know him? Yes, better than he knows himself.”
“Tell me, what is he?”
“His name is Talkative. He lives in our town. I’m surprised you don’t know him, though our town is large.”
“Whose son is he? And where does he live?”
“He is the son of one Saywell. He lived in Prattle Row, and everyone who knows him calls him Talkative of Prattle Row. For all his fine tongue, he’s a sorry fellow.”
“Well, he seems a very attractive man.”

“That is, to people who don’t know him well. He’s at his best away from home; close to home, he’s ugly enough. Your calling him attractive reminds me of something I’ve noticed about a painter’s work: some pictures look best from a distance, but up close they’re unpleasant.”
“I’m inclined to think you’re joking, since you smiled.”

“God forbid that I should joke about this, even if I smiled, or accuse anyone falsely! I’ll tell you more about him. This man is for any company and any talk. Just as he talks now with you, so he’ll talk on the bench at the alehouse; and the more drink he has in his head, the more of these things he has in his mouth. Religion has no place in his heart, or his house, or his conduct. Everything he has lies in his tongue, and his religion is to make a noise with it.”
“Do you say so? Then I’ve been badly deceived in this man.”

“Deceived? You can be sure of it. Remember the saying, ‘They talk, but they do not do.’ [Matt. 23:3] But the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. [1 Cor. 4:20] He talks of prayer, of repentance, of faith, and of the new birth, but he only knows how to talk about them. I’ve been in his household and watched him both at home and abroad, and I know what I’m saying is true. His house is as empty of religion as the white of an egg is of flavor. There is no prayer there, and no sign of repentance for sin; even an animal serves God better, in its way, than he does. He is the very stain and shame of religion to all who know him; because of him, religion can hardly get a good word in his whole end of town. [Rom. 2:24-25] The common people say of him, ‘A saint abroad and a devil at home,’ and his poor family finds it so. He is such a boor and a scold, and so unreasonable with his servants, that they don’t know how to work for him or speak to him. People who do business with him say they would get fairer treatment from a pirate, for he will cheat and outwit them if he can. He is raising his sons to follow in his steps. If he finds in any of them a ‘foolish timidity,’ which is what he calls the first stirrings of a tender conscience, he calls them fools and blockheads and won’t say a good word for them. I believe his wicked life has caused many to stumble and fall, and unless God prevents it, he will be the ruin of many more.”

“Well, my brother, I’m bound to believe you, not only because you say you know him, but because you report on people the way a Christian should. I can’t think you say these things out of ill will, but because they are simply true.”

“If I had known him no better than you, I might have thought what you did at first. And if this report had come only from enemies of religion, I would have taken it for slander, the kind that often falls from bad men’s mouths onto good men’s names. But I can prove from my own knowledge that he is guilty of all these things, and many more as bad. Besides, good people are ashamed of him. They can’t call him brother or friend; the mere mention of his name makes them blush.”
“Well, I see that saying and doing are two different things, and from now on I’ll pay more attention to the difference.”

“They are as different as the soul and the body. A body without a soul is only a corpse, and saying, by itself, is a corpse too. The soul of religion is the practical part. ‘Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.’ [James 1:27; see vv. 22-26] Talkative doesn’t understand this. He thinks hearing and saying make a good Christian, and so he deceives his own soul. Hearing is only the sowing of the seed; talking does not prove there is fruit in the heart and life. On the Day of Judgment people will be judged by their fruit. [Matt. 13; 25] It won’t be asked then, ‘Did you believe?’ but ‘Were you doers, or only talkers?’ The end of the world is compared to a harvest, and at harvest people care about nothing but the fruit. I don’t mean that anything can be accepted that does not come from faith. I say it only to show you how worthless Talkative’s profession will be on that day.”

“This brings to mind what Moses says about the animals that are clean. [Lev. 11:3-7; Deut. 14:6-8] A clean animal is one that both has a split hoof and chews the cud; not one that only has a split hoof, or only chews the cud. The hare chews the cud, but it is still unclean, because its hoof is not split. That is exactly like Talkative. He chews the cud: he seeks knowledge, he chews over the word. But he doesn’t split the hoof: he doesn’t part ways with sinners. Like the hare, he keeps the foot of a dog or a bear, and so he is unclean.”

“As far as I can tell, you’ve given the true gospel meaning of those passages. And I’ll add another thing. Paul calls some people, and great talkers too, a noisy gong and a clanging cymbal; or, as he puts it elsewhere, lifeless things that make a sound. [1 Cor. 13:1-3; 14:7] Lifeless, that is, without the true faith and grace of the gospel; and so they will never be given a place in the kingdom of heaven among the children of life, even though their talk sounds like the tongue of an angel.”
“Well, I wasn’t so fond of his company at first, but I’m sick of it now. What shall we do to get rid of him?”
“Take my advice and do as I tell you, and you’ll find he will soon be sick of your company too, unless God touches his heart and turns it.”
“What do you want me to do?”

“Go to him and begin a serious conversation about the power of religion. When he has approved of the subject, as he will, ask him plainly whether this power is at work in his heart, his house, and his conduct.”
So Faithful stepped forward again and said to Talkative, “Well, how are you? How are things now?”
“Fine, thank you. I thought we’d have had a great deal of talk by now.”
“Well, if you’re willing, let’s get to it now. Since you left it to me to choose the question, let it be this: How does the saving grace of God show itself when it is in a person’s heart?”

“I see that our talk is to be about the power of things. Well, it’s a very good question, and I’m happy to answer it. Here is my answer in brief. First, where the grace of God is in the heart, it causes a great outcry against sin. Second—”
“No, wait,” said Faithful. “Let’s take one at a time. I think you should rather say that it shows itself by making the soul hate its sin.”
“Why, what’s the difference between crying out against sin and hating it?”

“A great deal. A man may cry out against sin for appearances’ sake, but he cannot hate it except by a godly loathing of it. I’ve heard many people cry out against sin from the pulpit who can put up with it well enough in their hearts, their homes, and their lives. Joseph’s master’s wife cried out with a loud voice, as if she were very holy; yet for all that, she would gladly have committed adultery with him. Some people cry out against sin the way a mother scolds the child in her lap, calling her a naughty girl, and then starts hugging and kissing her.”
“You’re trying to trip me up, I see.”
“No, not at all. I only want to set things right. But what is the second thing by which you would show that a work of grace is in the heart?”
“Great knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel.”

“That sign should have come first. But first or last, it’s also false. A man may have great knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel and still have no work of grace in his soul. [1 Cor. 13] Even with all knowledge, he may be nothing, and so be no child of God. When Christ asked his disciples, ‘Do you understand all these things?’ and they said yes, he added, ‘Blessed are you if you do them.’ He puts the blessing not in knowing but in doing. For there is a knowledge that never turns into doing, like the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it. A man may know as much as an angel and still not be a Christian. To know is what pleases talkers and boasters; to do is what pleases God. I don’t mean the heart can be good without knowledge, for without it the heart is worthless. But there is knowledge and there is knowledge: knowledge that rests in bare speculation, and knowledge that comes with the grace of faith and love and moves a man to do the will of God from the heart. The first is enough for the talker; without the second, the true Christian is not content. ‘Give me understanding, and I will keep your law; I will obey it with my whole heart.’” [Ps. 119:34]
“You’re trying to trip me up again. This is not edifying.”
“Well, if you like, propose another sign of how this work of grace shows itself.”
“Not I, for I can see we won’t agree.”
“Then if you won’t, will you allow me to do it?”
“You’re free to do as you please.”
“A work of grace in the soul shows itself either to the person who has it, or to those who stand by and watch.

“To the person who has it, it shows itself like this. It convicts him of sin, especially of the corruption of his nature and the sin of unbelief, for which he knows he will be condemned unless he finds mercy at God’s hand through faith in Jesus Christ. [John 16:8; Rom. 7:24; John 16:9; Mark 16:16] Seeing and feeling this produces sorrow and shame for sin in him. He also finds revealed to him the Savior of the world, and his absolute need to take hold of him for life; and so he finds himself hungering and thirsting for him, and it is to that hunger and thirst that the promise is made. [Ps. 38:18; Jer. 31:19; Gal. 2:16; Acts 4:12; Matt. 5:6; Rev. 21:6] Then, according to how strong or weak his faith in his Savior is, so is his joy and peace, his love of holiness, his desire to know him better, and his desire to serve him in this world. Yet though it shows itself to him in this way, he is seldom able to conclude that it really is a work of grace, because his remaining sinfulness and his misused reason cause him to misjudge the matter. So the person who has this work needs very sound judgment before he can steadily conclude that it is a work of grace.
“To others, it shows itself like this:
“First, by a confession of his faith in Christ that comes from real experience. [Rom. 10:10; Phil. 1:27; Matt. 5:19]

“Second, by a life that matches that confession: a life of holiness, holiness of heart, holiness in his family, if he has one, and holiness in his conduct in the world. In general, this teaches him inwardly to hate his sin, and himself for it, in secret; to suppress it in his family; and to promote holiness in the world; not merely by talk, as a hypocrite or a talkative person may do, but by actually submitting, in faith and love, to the power of the Word. [John 14:15; Ps. 50:23; Job 42:5-6; Ezek. 20:43]
“And now, sir, if you have any objection to this short description of the work of grace and how it shows itself, raise it. If not, allow me to put a second question to you.”
“No, my part now is not to object but to listen. Let me have your second question.”

“It is this. Do you know the first part of this description from your own experience? And do your life and conduct bear witness to it? Or does your religion consist in word and tongue, and not in deed and truth? If you’re inclined to answer, please say nothing but what you know the God above will say amen to, and nothing but what your conscience can stand behind. For it is not the man who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. Besides, to say ‘I am this and that,’ when my conduct and all my neighbors tell me I’m lying, is great wickedness.”

At first Talkative began to blush. But he recovered himself and replied, “Now you appeal to experience, and conscience, and God, and call on him to confirm what is said. I didn’t expect this kind of conversation, and I’m not disposed to answer such questions. I don’t consider myself obliged to, unless you’ve appointed yourself my catechism teacher; and even if you have, I may still refuse to make you my judge. But tell me, why do you ask me such questions?”

“Because I saw you were eager to talk, and I didn’t know whether you had anything more than ideas. And to tell you the whole truth, I’ve heard that you are a man whose religion lies in talk, and that your conduct makes a liar of your mouth. They say you are a stain among Christians; that religion is worse off for your ungodly life; that some have already stumbled at your wicked ways, and more are in danger of being destroyed by them. Your religion, it seems, can live side by side with the alehouse, greed, impurity, swearing, lying, and worthless company. The saying about a prostitute, that she is a shame to all women, is true of you: you are a shame to all who profess the faith.”
“Since you’re so ready to believe rumors and to judge so rashly, I can only conclude that you are some sour or gloomy man, not fit to talk with. And so, goodbye.”

Then Christian came up and said to his brother, “I told you how it would go. Your words and his desires could not agree. He would rather leave your company than reform his life. But he’s gone, as I said; let him go. The loss is no one’s but his own. He has saved us the trouble of leaving him, for if he goes on as he is, as I suppose he will, he would only have been a blot on our company. Besides, the apostle says, ‘Withdraw yourself from such people.’”
“But I’m glad we had this little conversation with him,” said Faithful. “Perhaps he’ll think of it again. In any case, I have dealt plainly with him, and so I am clear of his blood if he perishes.”

“You did well to speak to him so plainly. There is very little of this faithful dealing nowadays, and that is why religion stinks in so many people’s nostrils. These talkative fools, whose religion is only words and whose lives are corrupt and empty, are so freely admitted into the fellowship of the godly that they puzzle the world, blemish Christianity, and grieve the sincere. I wish everyone would deal with them as you have. Then they would either be brought into line with true religion, or the company of the saints would become too hot for them.”
Then Faithful said:

v: How Talkative at first puts up his plumes!
How bravely he can speak! How he presumes
to drive down all before him! But as soon
as Faithful speaks of heart-work, like the moon
that’s past the full, into the wane he goes;
and so will all but one who heart-work knows.

blocks.p: So they went on, talking of what they had seen along the way, and so made easy a road that would otherwise, no doubt, have been tedious; for now they were going through a wilderness.
